title: Chemical stability, leaching, and failure modes of MIL-68-based materials in operating media: a mini-review
content: Operational stability, rather than initial adsorption or catalytic performance, remains the central bottleneck limiting the practical deployment of MIL-68-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). This work systematically synthesizes current understanding regarding the chemical stability, degradation pathways, and failure mechanisms of pristine, modified, composite, and derivative MIL-68 materials across liquid-phase separations, photocatalysis, and membrane/device applications. The analysis identifies that structural robustness is governed by the lability of metal–ligand coordination bonds (e.g., Al3+, In3+vs. Fe3+), node connectivity, linker substituent effects (e.g., –NH2 groups), and surface energy/roughness. Operational stressors trigger specific failure modes, including hydrolytic cleavage, metal/linker leaching, pore collapse, reactive oxygen species-mediated photo-corrosion, and interfacial voiding. While stabilization strategies (such as polymer matrix embedding, hydrophobic passivation, post-synthetic crosslinking, and heterojunction engineering) mitigate these failures, literature reporting remains inconsistent. Ultimately, this review establishes that maintaining short-term crystallinity or reusability is insufficient, underscoring the critical need for standardized, multi-technique durability testing under real-world operating conditions.
